Battle of Sayram (1627) — was an armed conflict in 1627 that took place in the vicinity of Sayram between two Kazakh khans Esim and Tursun, resulting in the latter's defeat.
Background
Between 1625 and 1627, a fragile balance of power was maintained between Tursun Muhammad and Esim Khan. Some historians believe that Esim Khan recognized Tursun's seniority as an elder Chingisid and showed him due respect [1]. During this period, the leaders temporarily reconciled and restored friendly ties [2]. However, deep-seated contradictions lurked behind this outward calm. One version suggests that Tursun Khan planned to use Oirat support to transfer the throne to Abulgazi, who had resided in Tashkent for a long time [3].
In 1627, Esim Khan organized a large-scale campaign against the Oirat uluses in Moghulistan, gathering troops from various tribes under his banners, including a portion of the Katagans [5]. Researchers suggest that this maneuver may have been a deliberate provocation. Esim Khan likely anticipated that the attack on the Oirats would push Tursun toward retaliatory aggression. In such a scenario, Esim Khan would appear to society as a victimized defender of the faith, while Tursun would be seen as a traitor allied with infidels [3]. Taking advantage of Esim Khan's absence, Tursun Khan violated their agreements and the code of honor [6]. While Esim Khan's main forces were away on the campaign, Tursun directed his troops toward Esim's headquarters in Turkestan with orders to completely devastate it [7]. The attackers ransacked the camp, killed many people, and took Esim Khan's family and children captive, transporting them to Tashkent [2].
Battle
Esim Khan cut his campaign short and hastily returned to Tashkent [8], while Tursun Muhammad Khan personally led his army to meet his rival, intending to crush him [7]. The opposing forces met in the vicinity of Sayram, north of the city, and «kindled the furnace of battle» [9]. In the course of the engagement, Tursun Khan's army suffered a defeat [7], and he was forced to flee the battlefield and retreat to Tashkent with the remnants of his forces [8][9].
Further Events
By the time Tursun returned, Tashkent and its surroundings had been seized by the Ashtarkhanids with the support of Ablai Sultan. Esim Khan advanced from Sayram toward Tashkent, pursuing Tursun Muhammad. Through the mediator Bek-ogly, he formed an alliance with the ruler of Bukhara. During this time, Tursun Muhammad's own associates killed him, and Esim Khan delivered the deceased's head to Imam Quli Khan as a gesture of friendship. In response, the ruler of the Bukhara Khanate officially confirmed Esim Khan's right to possess Tashkent, Turkestan, and the adjacent lands [7].
Esim Khan's second period of reign was brief but historically significant. Realizing the danger of internal strife, the Khan sought to strengthen central authority. Tribes capable of supporting the separatism of the sultans were either weakened or eliminated. To ensure public order, Esim Khan initiated the creation of a single body of laws for all Kazakhs. This code went down in history under the name "Esim Khannyn Eski Zholy" (The Ancient Path of Esim Khan) [2].
